title: Can the Nodes Be Painted in Two Colours?

concept.title: Colour a node, then give its neighbours the other colour; a clash means an odd cycle
body: Can every node be painted red or blue so that **every edge joins a red and a blue node**? Such a graph is called *bipartite* (two-sided). Think of a class where every friendship is between a boy and a girl, or of tasks that must be shared between two workers so that conflicting tasks go to different workers.

Try it by force, because the colours are forced: paint a start node red; all its neighbours must be blue; their neighbours red; and so on. This is a breadth-first search that **alternates the colour at every step**. If a node ever has to be both colours, that is, an edge joins two nodes of the **same colour**, then two colours are not enough. (This happens exactly when the graph has a cycle of **odd length**, like a triangle.)

body.code:
color = [-1] * (n + 1)                 # -1 means "not painted yet"
ok = True
for start in range(1, n + 1):          # the graph may have several components
    if color[start] != -1:
        continue
    color[start] = 0
    queue = [start]
    for v in queue:
        for w in adj[v]:
            if color[w] == -1:
                color[w] = 1 - color[v]
                queue.append(w)
            elif color[w] == color[v]:     # an edge inside one colour
                ok = False

body: Each component is started separately, because they do not affect each other. The time is O(n + m). The colour array also works as the "seen" array.

statement: An undirected graph has `n` nodes and `m` edges. Can every node be painted with one of two colours so that the two ends of every edge have different colours? Print `yes` or `no`.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n) and the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: an edge between the nodes `u` and `v`.
constraints: There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.

examples.note: A cycle of four nodes: paint 1 and 3 red, 2 and 4 blue: yes.
A triangle needs three colours: no.

hints: Paint the start node 0, its neighbours 1, their neighbours 0, and so on.
If an edge joins two nodes of the same colour, the answer is no.
Start a new search for every component that is not painted yet.

solution.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).
